attributes.title: Level 3

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use comments to create 2 sections in the editor to better organize your code?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What symbol tells the program to skip over the text on a line?

❓ How do you create blank lines in the JavaScript editor?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡  Explain to the ninja that typing // tells the project to skip over the text that follows and move onto the next line of code. Just as when naming sprites, it’s useful to be short and descriptive when describing comments.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by adding code comments to organize where the code will go in the editor!


Type // set up on line 1 of the editor. Press the Enter key a few times to create several blank lines, then type // sprite creation.


In JavaScript, // signals a code comment and the text that follows will appear in green. This text will be skipped over when the project is run.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you click the palette to select a background image for this project?
steps.instructions:
Choose a background for the screen saver project! 


Add a background image to this project. Open Scene, drag [set background image to (img)] under // set up.  

Click the palette to the left of the line of code to choose a background image from the Gallery.


Click ▶ to see the background image appear on the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you type quotation marks around the strings inside the parentheses of game.splash(text)?
steps.instructions:
Add a title to the screen saver project.


Open Game, drag [splash (title)] under // set up underneath the existing code. 


The game.splash function takes 2 parameters: a title and a subtitle. Replace null with a string inside of quotation marks that tells the user about the project theme. Use a comma , to add a second parameter with a subtitle.


Click ▶ to see the title and subtitle appear on screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you choose an effect by typing . after effects and selecting a property from the code completion tool?
steps.instructions:
Add a screen effect to the screen saver project.


Open Scene, drag [start screen (effect) effect] under // set up underneath the existing code.


Change the effect by deleting .blizzard and retyping . after effects to open the code completion tool. Scroll down the list to the properties then select one that fits the theme of the screen saver.  


The startScreenEffect function takes 2 parameters: duration and particlesPerSecond. Inside the parentheses, fill in the 2 parameters with number arguments, separated by commas, to customize the screen effect. Use the documentation box for help with each parameter. Type null  to skip a parameter.


Click ▶ to see the screen effect appear on screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update the vx and vy parameters so that the projectile moves from one side of the screen across to the other?
steps.instructions:
Use a projectile to create a sprite that moves from one side of the screen to the other!


Open Sprites and drag [projectile (img) from side with vx (vx) vy (vy)] underneath // sprite creation. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

let projectile = sprites.createProjectileFromSide
(img`...`, 50, 50)

The createProjectileFromSide function takes 3 parameters: image, x velocity (vx) and y velocity (vy). Click the palette to the left of the line of code to choose a sprite from the Gallery. Update the vx and vy arguments (50, 50) so that the sprite moves across the screen in a straight line by typing a positive or negative value for vx and 0 for vy.


Click ▶ to see the projectile sprite appear and move across the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you cut (Ctrl + X) and paste (Ctrl + V) the projectile’s code inside the curly brackets { } of game.onUpdateInterval?
steps.instructions:
Use a loop to make multiple projectile sprites appear!


Open Game and drag [run code on game update every (period) ms] under // sprite creation underneath the projectile code. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

game.onUpdateInterval(500, function() { … })

In JavaScript, curly brackets { } are used to create block statements, or indented lines of code that will run inside of another line of code, such as an event or loop. The curly brackets create a “container” for the block statement, like the containers used in the blocks editor.


The argument 500 tells the loop how often, in milliseconds (ms), to run the code inside the curly brackets { }. It can be updated to different values to make the code run more or less often.


Highlight all of the projectile code, then press Ctrl + X at the same time to cut this entire section of code. Click on the blank line between the curly brackets { } and press Ctrl + V to paste the projectile code inside the loop. 


Click ▶ to see the projectile sprites appear and move across the screen, over and over again.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you type the projectile sprite’s name in the projecile.y = value code and update the value to randomly select from a range of integers?
steps.instructions:
Change the starting position of the projectile by adding randomness to the project!


Press the Enter key after the projectile’s code to create a new blank line inside the curly brackets { }. On the new blank line, type the projectile sprite’s name, followed by a dot operator . and the y property from the code completion tool. Then, add a space and an assignment operator (=) next to the property. In JavaScript, a single equal sign (=) is called an assignment operator because it assigns a value to something.


Open Math and drag [randint] next to the assignment operator to set y to a random integer, or number. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 

randint(0, 10)

The randint function takes 2 parameters, the minimum and maximum value of possible integers to choose from. Keep the minimum value at 0. Replace the maximum value 10 by typing screen.height. This means that the program will randomly choose a number between 0 and the screen height value (120) for the y coordinate of the projectile sprite.


Click ▶ to see the projectile sprites appear at different y coordinates and move across the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you switch back to the blocks editor? What looks similar and what looks different?
steps.instructions:
Test out the project. Does it work as expected?


Switch to the blocks editor to see what the JavaScript code looks like in blocks! Notice what is similar about the code, and what looks different: how does the block statement inside the curly brackets appear in blocks, versus in JavaScript?

subgroups.title: Screen Saver
subgroups.introduction: Create a screen saver project in JavaScript that uses projectiles inside the block statement of a loop to create an ongoing scene!

validationItems.text: Use a splash screen with a custom message.
Use a screen effect with 2 parameters.
Use a game on update interval loop.
Use screen.height to randomize the position of the projectile.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 3 of Blue Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about block statements. In JavaScript, instead of adding code into different containers, you’ll add block statements inside curly brackets { } of an event or a loop. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 3:

badges.title: Thinking Inside the Block
badges.description: Use block statements inside curly brackets { } to add code inside of events and loops.

badges.title: Projectile Manager
badges.description: Create a  projectile in JavaScript.

badges.title: Game On (Update Interval)
badges.description: Use a game update loop in JavaScript.

badges.title: About Yay High
badges.description: Use the screen object’s height property instead of a number.

badges.title: Framing the Discussion
badges.description: Use setDialogFrame to design a custom text box.

badges.title: Settle the Score
badges.description: Set the score in JavaScript.

badges.title: Cute as a Button
badges.description: Use a button event in JavaScript.
